question.text: How does the manual say driving skills are gained?

answer.text: Driving skills come only through practice and experience, and the manual offers these tips as things to practice to become a safer, more skillful driver.

teaching.text: The manual is clear that driving skill only comes with practice and experience, so these tips are habits to rehearse. Remember: Practice builds skill.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving skills come only through practice and experience, and the manual offers these tips as things to practice to become a safer, more skillful driver.

question.text: What must you know before starting and while driving?

answer.text: Before starting the vehicle and while driving, you must know what is happening around you by looking ahead, to the sides and behind.

teaching.text: Before you start and while you drive, keep track of what is happening ahead, to the sides and behind you. Remember: Ahead, sides and behind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before starting the vehicle and while driving, you must know what is happening around you by looking ahead, to the sides and behind.

question.text: What eye habit should you develop for every drive?

answer.text: Develop a searching pattern for your eyes and use it every time you drive.

teaching.text: Build a regular searching pattern for your eyes and repeat it every time you drive. Remember: Same search pattern every drive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Develop a searching pattern for your eyes and use it every time you drive.

question.text: Why should you keep your eyes moving instead of staring?

answer.text: Searching shows you situations that could become a problem and gives you time to change your speed or road position, so keep your eyes moving instead of staring at any one thing.

teaching.text: Moving your eyes instead of staring lets you spot trouble early and gives you time to change speed or position. Remember: Moving eyes spot trouble.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Searching shows you situations that could become a problem and gives you time to change your speed or road position, so keep your eyes moving instead of staring at any one thing.

question.text: What does looking well down your planned path give you?

answer.text: Looking well down your planned path gives you time to adjust and plan, leads to better decisions and may spare you from emergency braking and steering.

teaching.text: Looking far down your planned path buys time to plan, improves your decisions and may save you from emergency braking or steering. Remember: Look far, plan ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Looking well down your planned path gives you time to adjust and plan, leads to better decisions and may spare you from emergency braking and steering.

question.text: How far ahead should you ideally watch?

answer.text: Ideally, try to watch what is happening twenty to thirty seconds ahead of your vehicle.

teaching.text: Try to keep watch on what is happening twenty to thirty seconds ahead of your vehicle. Remember: Twenty to thirty seconds ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Ideally, try to watch what is happening twenty to thirty seconds ahead of your vehicle.

question.text: How can you keep from limiting how far you can see?

answer.text: Avoid situations that cut how far you can see, such as following a larger vehicle too closely, and adjust your speed and road position to see best.

teaching.text: Stay out of situations that block your view, like tailgating a larger vehicle, and set your speed and lane position to see best. Remember: Do not hide behind trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid situations that cut how far you can see, such as following a larger vehicle too closely, and adjust your speed and road position to see best.

question.text: How does your sight distance in a city compare with a highway?

answer.text: How far ahead you can look depends on where you drive, and in cities and urban areas you may not see as far as on a highway.

teaching.text: Sight distance depends on where you drive; in cities you may not see as far ahead as on a highway. Remember: Cities shorten your view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: How far ahead you can look depends on where you drive, and in cities and urban areas you may not see as far as on a highway.

question.text: Why should you search to the sides of your vehicle?

answer.text: Search to the sides of your vehicle to see whether other road users are about to cross your path.

teaching.text: Check to the sides as well, so you notice road users who are about to cross your path. Remember: Watch for cross traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Search to the sides of your vehicle to see whether other road users are about to cross your path.

question.text: When is it especially important to check traffic behind you?

answer.text: Stay aware of traffic behind you, using your mirrors, especially when you change lanes, slow down or stop, or enter an intersection.

teaching.text: Use your mirrors to track traffic behind you, especially before changing lanes, slowing, stopping or entering an intersection. Remember: Mirrors before changes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay aware of traffic behind you, using your mirrors, especially when you change lanes, slow down or stop, or enter an intersection.

question.text: What does driving at a safe speed involve?

answer.text: Driving safely means adjusting your speed to road and traffic conditions, keeping an adequate following distance and obeying the speed limits that apply.

teaching.text: A safe speed fits the road and traffic, keeps a proper following gap and stays within the posted limits. Remember: Conditions, gap, limits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving safely means adjusting your speed to road and traffic conditions, keeping an adequate following distance and obeying the speed limits that apply.

question.text: When should you slow down for a curve, and to what speed?

answer.text: Always slow down before you enter a curve, to a safe speed that lets you apply slight and constant acceleration all the way through it.

teaching.text: Slow down before a curve to a speed that lets you accelerate gently and steadily all the way through it. Remember: Slow before the curve.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always slow down before you enter a curve, to a safe speed that lets you apply slight and constant acceleration all the way through it.

question.text: When should you slow even more for a curve?

answer.text: Slow down even more on a curve when traction is poor, when you are following other vehicles and when you cannot see where the curve ends.

teaching.text: Slow even more for a curve when traction is poor, when you are following others or when you cannot see its end. Remember: Poor grip, followers, blind curves.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow down even more on a curve when traction is poor, when you are following other vehicles and when you cannot see where the curve ends.

question.text: Why should you brake before a curve rather than in it?

answer.text: Speed should come down before the curve, because hard braking after you have entered it could make the tires lose traction.

teaching.text: Get your speed down before the curve, because braking hard once you are in it can make the tires lose grip. Remember: Brake early, keep traction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Speed should come down before the curve, because hard braking after you have entered it could make the tires lose traction.

question.text: When should you reduce speed in bad weather?

answer.text: Reduce your speed at the first sign of rain, snow, sleet or ice.

teaching.text: Ease off the moment rain, snow, sleet or ice begins. Remember: First drops, slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reduce your speed at the first sign of rain, snow, sleet or ice.

question.text: How does a slippery road affect stopping and turning?

answer.text: On a slippery road your tires grip less, so stopping takes longer and turning without skidding is harder.

teaching.text: Slippery roads mean less tire grip, longer stops and a greater risk of skidding in turns. Remember: Less grip, longer stops.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a slippery road your tires grip less, so stopping takes longer and turning without skidding is harder.

question.text: What is hydroplaning?

answer.text: Hydroplaning is when your steering tires end up riding on a film of water above the road surface, much like water skis.

teaching.text: Hydroplaning happens when the steering tires ride up on a layer of water, much like water skis. Remember: Tires skiing on water.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hydroplaning is when your steering tires end up riding on a film of water above the road surface, much like water skis.

question.text: What is the best way to avoid hydroplaning?

answer.text: The best way to avoid losing traction to hydroplaning is to slow down in the rain or on roads with pooled water or puddles.

teaching.text: Slowing down in rain and on roads with standing water or puddles is the best defense against hydroplaning. Remember: Slow down in the rain.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The best way to avoid losing traction to hydroplaning is to slow down in the rain or on roads with pooled water or puddles.

question.text: What should you do if a road ahead is flooded or barricaded?

answer.text: If you see a flooded road, or barricades blocking one, find another route to where you are going.

teaching.text: When a road is flooded or barricaded, choose another route. Remember: Turn around, find another way.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you see a flooded road, or barricades blocking one, find another route to where you are going.

question.text: How quickly can flash floods arrive?

answer.text: Flash floods can come quickly and without warning, within a few minutes or hours of excessive rainfall.

teaching.text: Flash floods arrive fast and without warning, sometimes within minutes or hours of heavy rain. Remember: Floods can come in minutes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Flash floods can come quickly and without warning, within a few minutes or hours of excessive rainfall.

question.text: What can cause flooding on roads?

answer.text: Flooding can come from rivers and streams overflowing, dams or levees breaking, run-off from deep snow or any heavy rainfall, and floodwater gathers on roads, bridges and low areas.

teaching.text: Floods can come from overflowing rivers and streams, failed dams or levees, melting deep snow or heavy rain, and they collect on roads, bridges and low ground. Remember: Rivers, dams, snow, rain.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Flooding can come from rivers and streams overflowing, dams or levees breaking, run-off from deep snow or any heavy rainfall, and floodwater gathers on roads, bridges and low areas.

question.text: Why take special care around possible flooding at night?

answer.text: Take special care at night around possible flooding, when visibility is limited.

teaching.text: Be especially careful about possible flooding at night, when you cannot see as well. Remember: Night hides the water.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Take special care at night around possible flooding, when visibility is limited.

question.text: What can six inches of water do to most passenger cars?

answer.text: Six inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling.

teaching.text: Just six inches of water can reach the underside of most cars and cause stalling or loss of control. Remember: Six inches can stall you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Six inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling.

question.text: What can two feet of moving water do?

answer.text: Two feet of moving water can sweep away most vehicles, including sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks.

teaching.text: Two feet of moving water can carry away most vehicles, even SUVs and pickups. Remember: Two feet sweeps cars away.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Two feet of moving water can sweep away most vehicles, including sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks.

question.text: How do the six-inch and two-foot water depths differ in danger?

answer.text: Six inches of water is enough to reach the underside of most passenger cars, while two feet of moving water can carry away even SUVs and pickups.

teaching.text: Six inches can reach a car's underside, while two feet of moving water can carry the whole vehicle away. Remember: Stall at six, float at two.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Six inches of water is enough to reach the underside of most passenger cars, while two feet of moving water can carry away even SUVs and pickups.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Stall at six, float at two

question.text: Why should you never cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow?

answer.text: Never try to cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow, because the water can hide dips and other hazards and can wash away the road's underlying surface.

teaching.text: Do not try to cross floodwater even when it looks shallow, since it can hide dips and wash out the road underneath. Remember: Hidden dips, missing road.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never try to cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow, because the water can hide dips and other hazards and can wash away the road's underlying surface.

question.text: What should you do if there is no other route around floodwater?

answer.text: If no other route exists, drive to higher ground and wait for the floodwater to go down.

teaching.text: With no other way around, head to higher ground and wait for the water to drop. Remember: Higher ground, then wait.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If no other route exists, drive to higher ground and wait for the floodwater to go down.

question.text: What is total stopping distance?

answer.text: Total stopping distance is how far your vehicle travels, in ideal conditions, from the moment you realize you must stop until it actually stops.

teaching.text: Total stopping distance runs from the instant you realize you must stop to the moment the vehicle stops, in ideal conditions. Remember: Notice to full stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Total stopping distance is how far your vehicle travels, in ideal conditions, from the moment you realize you must stop until it actually stops.

question.text: How does speed affect stopping?

answer.text: The faster you are going, the more time and distance you need to stop.

teaching.text: The more speed you carry, the more time and distance it takes to stop. Remember: Faster means farther.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The faster you are going, the more time and distance you need to stop.

question.text: What is perception time, and how long does it average?

answer.text: Perception time is the time and distance it takes to recognize that you must stop, and for an alert driver it averages three quarters second to one second.

teaching.text: Perception time is how long it takes to recognize that you must stop, about three-quarters of a second to one second for an alert driver. Remember: Seeing the need to stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Perception time is the time and distance it takes to recognize that you must stop, and for an alert driver it averages three quarters second to one second.

question.text: What is reaction time, and how long does it average?

answer.text: Reaction time is the time and distance it takes to move your foot from the gas pedal and start braking, and it averages three quarters second to one second.

teaching.text: Reaction time is how long it takes to move your foot from the gas to the brake, also about three-quarters of a second to one second. Remember: Moving the foot to brake.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reaction time is the time and distance it takes to move your foot from the gas pedal and start braking, and it averages three quarters second to one second.

question.text: How do perception time and reaction time differ?

answer.text: Perception time is about recognizing that you must stop, while reaction time is about moving your foot from the gas to the brake, and both average three quarters second to one second.

teaching.text: First you perceive the need to stop, then you react by moving to the brake, and each step takes about three-quarters of a second to one second. Remember: Recognize, then react.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Perception time is about recognizing that you must stop, while reaction time is about moving your foot from the gas to the brake, and both average three quarters second to one second.

question.text: What is braking distance, and how far does it take at highway speed?

answer.text: Braking distance is the time and distance your brakes need to stop the vehicle, about one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes.

teaching.text: Braking distance is how far the brakes need to stop you, about one hundred fifty-eight feet from fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes. Remember: Brakes need room too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Braking distance is the time and distance your brakes need to stop the vehicle, about one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes.

question.text: What is a space cushion, and why keep one?

answer.text: The more space you leave between you and other road users, the more time you have to react; this space is called a space cushion, and you should keep one all around your vehicle.

teaching.text: A space cushion is the room you keep all around your vehicle, and more room means more time to react. Remember: Space buys reaction time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The more space you leave between you and other road users, the more time you have to react; this space is called a space cushion, and you should keep one all around your vehicle.

question.text: What happens when you follow the vehicle ahead too closely?

answer.text: Following the vehicle ahead too closely limits your view of the road and leaves too little time to react and avoid a collision.

teaching.text: Tailgating cuts your view of the road and leaves too little time to react and avoid a collision. Remember: Too close, too little time.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Following the vehicle ahead too closely limits your view of the road and leaves too little time to react and avoid a collision.

question.text: What minimum following distance should you keep?

answer.text: Always try to keep a following distance of at least four seconds behind the vehicle in front.

teaching.text: Keep at least four seconds of following distance behind the vehicle ahead. Remember: Four seconds minimum.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always try to keep a following distance of at least four seconds behind the vehicle in front.

question.text: How do you count your following distance?

answer.text: To check the gap, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a sign, pole or other fixed point, then count one thousand one, one thousand two and so on until you reach that point.

teaching.text: To measure the gap, watch the car ahead pass a fixed object, then count one thousand one, one thousand two, until you reach it. Remember: Fixed point, then count.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To check the gap, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a sign, pole or other fixed point, then count one thousand one, one thousand two and so on until you reach that point.

question.text: What do you do if you reach the fixed point before counting to four?

answer.text: If you reach the fixed point before counting to one thousand four, you are too close, so slow down and count again at another point until the gap is at least four seconds.

teaching.text: If you reach the object before one thousand four, you are too close, so slow down and recount until you have four seconds. Remember: Too soon, back off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you reach the fixed point before counting to one thousand four, you are too close, so slow down and count again at another point until the gap is at least four seconds.

question.text: How can you practice judging the four-second gap?

answer.text: You can test how well you judge the four-second gap by guessing how many seconds away an object is and then counting the seconds it takes to reach it.

teaching.text: Practice judging the gap by guessing how many seconds away an object is, then counting to check yourself. Remember: Guess, then count.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You can test how well you judge the four-second gap by guessing how many seconds away an object is and then counting the seconds it takes to reach it.

question.text: When should you increase following distance on the road surface?

answer.text: Increase your following distance on slippery roads.

teaching.text: On slippery roads, leave a bigger following gap. Remember: Slippery means more room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Increase your following distance on slippery roads.

question.text: When else should you leave extra following room?

answer.text: Also leave more room at night, in fog or bad weather, behind vehicles that must stop at railroad crossings such as transit buses, school buses and hazardous materials carriers, and behind large vehicles like trucks, buses, RVs and vehicles towing trailers.

teaching.text: Leave extra room at night, in fog or bad weather, behind buses and hazardous materials carriers that stop at railroad crossings, and behind large vehicles. Remember: Night, fog, big rigs, buses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Also leave more room at night, in fog or bad weather, behind vehicles that must stop at railroad crossings such as transit buses, school buses and hazardous materials carriers, and behind large vehicles like trucks, buses, RVs and vehicles towing trailers.

question.text: Why should you avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches?

answer.text: Avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches, because you may sit in their blind spot and lose the side space you might need to avoid a crash.

teaching.text: Do not ride alongside other vehicles for long, because you may be in their blind spot and short of escape room. Remember: Do not ride in blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches, because you may sit in their blind spot and lose the side space you might need to avoid a crash.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Do not ride in blind spots

question.text: How should you position yourself relative to the centerline?

answer.text: Do not crowd the centerline, and keep as much room as you can between you and oncoming traffic.

teaching.text: Stay off the centerline and keep as much room as you can from oncoming traffic. Remember: Give oncoming traffic room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not crowd the centerline, and keep as much room as you can between you and oncoming traffic.

question.text: How can you help vehicles joining a multi-lane road?

answer.text: Make room for vehicles joining a multi-lane or limited access road by moving over a lane or adjusting your speed.

teaching.text: Help vehicles joining a multi-lane or limited access road by moving over a lane or adjusting your speed. Remember: Make room for mergers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Make room for vehicles joining a multi-lane or limited access road by moving over a lane or adjusting your speed.

question.text: Who deserves extra space on the road?

answer.text: Give pedestrians extra space, especially children, elderly people and bicyclists.

teaching.text: Give people on foot extra room, especially children, older people and bicyclists. Remember: Walkers, kids, elders, cyclists.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Give pedestrians extra space, especially children, elderly people and bicyclists.

question.text: What should you do when a tractor trailer passes you?

answer.text: When a tractor trailer passes you, give it more room by moving to the outer part of your lane, away from the truck.

teaching.text: When a tractor trailer passes, move to the far side of your lane to give it more room. Remember: Drift away from the truck.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a tractor trailer passes you, give it more room by moving to the outer part of your lane, away from the truck.

question.text: How can you help the driver behind you keep a safe distance?

answer.text: You can help the driver behind you keep a safe distance by holding a steady speed, signaling early and leaving extra room ahead before you slow down or turn.

teaching.text: Keep a steady speed, signal early and leave extra room ahead so the driver behind you can follow safely. Remember: Steady, early signals, room ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You can help the driver behind you keep a safe distance by holding a steady speed, signaling early and leaving extra room ahead before you slow down or turn.

question.text: When do headlights especially help others see you?

answer.text: Headlights help others see you, especially on rainy, snowy or foggy days, when you should use low beams and slow down, and as it gets dark or when you drive away from a rising or setting sun.

teaching.text: Headlights help others see you, especially in rain, snow or fog, at dusk and when the sun is low behind you. Remember: Lights on to be seen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights help others see you, especially on rainy, snowy or foggy days, when you should use low beams and slow down, and as it gets dark or when you drive away from a rising or setting sun.

question.text: Which lights should you use on rainy, snowy or foggy days?

answer.text: On rainy, snowy or foggy days the manual says to drive with your low-beam lights on and to slow down.

teaching.text: In rain, snow or fog, drive with low beams on and slow down. Remember: Low beams in bad weather.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On rainy, snowy or foggy days the manual says to drive with your low-beam lights on and to slow down.

question.text: When is a light horn tap useful?

answer.text: A light horn tap is useful when pedestrians or bicyclists seem to be moving into your lane, when you pass a driver who starts turning into your lane, or when a driver is not paying attention or may not see you.

teaching.text: A light horn tap helps when walkers or cyclists drift toward your lane, when someone turns into your lane as you pass, or when a driver may not see you. Remember: Tap to warn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A light horn tap is useful when pedestrians or bicyclists seem to be moving into your lane, when you pass a driver who starts turning into your lane, or when a driver is not paying attention or may not see you.

question.text: How much horn is normally enough?

answer.text: Under normal circumstances a light tap on the horn should be all you need.

teaching.text: Normally, a light tap on the horn is all you need. Remember: A light tap will do.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under normal circumstances a light tap on the horn should be all you need.

question.text: When should you use the horn, and when not?

answer.text: Use the horn only to communicate, since misuse can scare or anger other road users, and do not use it near blind pedestrians.

teaching.text: Use the horn only to communicate, because misuse can startle or anger people, and never near blind pedestrians. Remember: Horn only to communicate.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Use the horn only to communicate, since misuse can scare or anger other road users, and do not use it near blind pedestrians.

question.text: Should you use the horn near blind pedestrians?

answer.text: The horn is a tool for getting attention when needed, but near blind pedestrians it should not be used at all.

teaching.text: The horn can get attention when needed, but do not use it at all near a blind pedestrian. Remember: Never near blind walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The horn is a tool for getting attention when needed, but near blind pedestrians it should not be used at all.

question.text: How far ahead does South Carolina law require a turn signal?

answer.text: South Carolina law requires a turn signal at least one hundred feet before you change lanes, turn left or right, or merge into traffic.

teaching.text: State law requires your turn signal at least one hundred feet before you change lanes, turn or merge. Remember: Signal one hundred feet ahead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: South Carolina law requires a turn signal at least one hundred feet before you change lanes, turn left or right, or merge into traffic.

question.text: What should you do with your signal after a lane change or turn?

answer.text: Once a lane change, turn or merge is finished, cancel your signal so other drivers are not confused.

teaching.text: When the lane change, turn or merge is done, cancel the signal so you do not confuse others. Remember: Cancel when done.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Once a lane change, turn or merge is finished, cancel your signal so other drivers are not confused.

question.text: When should you signal before slowing down?

answer.text: Brake lights tell others you are slowing, and you should signal before slowing when turning off a road that has no separate turn or exit lane, or when parking or turning just before an intersection.

teaching.text: Brake lights warn that you are slowing, and you should also signal before slowing to turn off a road with no turn lane or to park or turn just before an intersection. Remember: Signal before slowing off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Brake lights tell others you are slowing, and you should signal before slowing when turning off a road that has no separate turn or exit lane, or when parking or turning just before an intersection.

question.text: Are brake lights enough when you slow to leave a road with no turn lane?

answer.text: Brake lights show you are slowing, but you should also signal before slowing when you leave a road that has no separate turn or exit lane.

teaching.text: Brake lights alone are not enough when you slow to leave a road without a turn or exit lane; signal first. Remember: Brake lights plus a signal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Brake lights show you are slowing, but you should also signal before slowing when you leave a road that has no separate turn or exit lane.

hooks_spoken: Keep your eyes moving in a searching pattern, look twenty to thirty seconds ahead, and check the mirrors before changing speed or lanes.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of visual search. Keep your eyes moving in a searching pattern, look twenty to thirty seconds ahead, and check the mirrors before changing speed or lanes. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of speed for curves and wet roads. Slow down before curves and at the first sign of rain, and slow in wet weather to avoid hydroplaning. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of flooded roads. Never drive into floodwater: six inches can stall a car and two feet of moving water can sweep it away. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of stopping distance. Stopping takes perception time, reaction time and braking distance, and every bit of it grows with speed. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Keep at least four seconds behind the car ahead, counting from a fixed point, and add more in poor conditions.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of following distance. Keep at least four seconds behind the car ahead, counting from a fixed point, and add more in poor conditions. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of side and rear space. Do not linger beside other vehicles, stay off the centerline and give pedestrians and bicyclists extra room. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Signal at least one hundred feet before you move, use low beams in bad weather, and use the horn only to communicate.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of communicating with others. Signal at least one hundred feet before you move, use low beams in bad weather, and use the horn only to communicate. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.
